page: The Vultr vc2-4c-8gb is an entry-tier virtual instance within the Cloud Compute family, providing 4 shared vCPUs mapped across 2 physical cores on an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor clocked at 2.0 GHz. The hardware configuration includes 8.0 GB of system memory, providing an allocation ratio of 2.0 GB per vCPU. The instance is bundled with 160 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No dedicated hardware GPUs are present in this configuration.

Benchmark results place the processing and memory capabilities primarily in the lower quartiles. The single-core Geekbench score of 936.0 and PassMark memory score of 1173.18 place the instance within the bottom 10 percent of recorded systems. Multi-core performance scales modestly, achieving a Geekbench multi-core result of 2888.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 4794.79. Memory bandwidth tests demonstrate 24.41 GB/sec for uncached read-only large blocks and 19.55 GB/sec for uncached write operations, while cached read-only access reaches 367.64 GB/sec.

Given its shared CPU allocation model and lower-tier throughput metrics, the vc2-4c-8gb offers baseline resource density suited for low-utilization environments. Key tradeoffs involve modest single-thread compute capabilities and slower uncached memory access, which limit suitability for high-throughput or compute-heavy processing. The instance fits lightweight workloads such as entry-level web serving, dev-test environments, low-volume background tasks, and small internal utility services.

It includes 8.0 GB of RAM (2.0 GB per core) and bundles 160 GB of local NVMe SSD storage along with a single complimentary public IPv4 address. Benchmarks position the instance primarily in the lower performance brackets, with a Geekbench single-core score of 936.0, multi-core score of 2888.0, and PassMark CPU score of 4794.79. The shared CPU profile presents lower compute density and memory throughput, rendering the server best matched to budget-conscious workloads, general development environments, low-traffic static web servers, and lightweight utility tasks.
